title: The Maccabees (1 Maccabees 4:36–59)
hook: after a desecration, the temple is cleansed and rededicated, the feast Jesus later attends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tobit and the angel, a guide on the road nobody recognized. Your line was an angel on the road. Who did you travel kindly with? Day seven hundred forty-five.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch." That's John's Gospel, chapter ten. It drops a festival into the story without explaining it. Which feast is that, and what was being dedicated? The answer is in a book written about a time when the temple had been taken from the people. A foreign king, Antiochus, had set an abomination on the altar and forced sacrifices the law forbade. A priest named Mattathias and his sons resisted, and in time his son Judas, called Maccabeus, led them. Today they've just won, and they walk up to the temple to see what's left.

First Maccabees is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and some Protestant Bibles print it among the Apocrypha. Its account is vivid. Judas says to his brothers, in effect: our enemies are beaten, let us go up to cleanse and dedicate the sanctuary. They climb Mount Zion and find the sanctuary desolate, the altar profaned, the gates burned, and shrubs growing in the courts like a forest or a hillside. Their first response isn't to start scrubbing. They tear their clothes, put ashes on their heads, and fall on their faces. Grief comes first. Then the work. They choose priests who had kept the law. They take down the defiled altar, and here's a striking detail: they don't know what to do with its stones. So they store them on the temple mount until a prophet should come and tell them. They don't pretend to have an answer they don't have. They build a new altar of whole stones, make new holy vessels, light the lamps on the lampstand, and set out the bread. And early one morning they offer sacrifice on the new altar, with songs, harps and cymbals, and all the people fall on their faces and worship. Then Judas and the whole congregation decide that the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept every year, for eight days, with joy and gladness. That feast is Hanukkah, the Hebrew word for dedication, and Jewish tradition keeps it with lights for eight nights. Jewish tradition also tells a later story about a small jar of oil that lasted; 1 Maccabees itself doesn't tell that story. It tells of an altar rebuilt and a people giving the space back to God. And John's Gospel shows Jesus walking in that temple on that feast, in winter.

Here's the practice: rededicate one small space. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that was meant for good and got overgrown or misused: a room that's become a dumping ground, a morning hour lost to your phone, a friendship gone sour, a habit that used to be prayer and is now just noise. Like the Maccabees, let yourself be sad about it first. Then choose the one thing you'd clear and give back. If you pray, you can give it back to God in your own words. If you don't, just name what it's for again. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication: the feast that remembers the temple cleansed and its altar rededicated, kept for eight days, and the feast of the dedication John's Gospel names.
Your line: rededicate. Today, light one light, a candle or a lamp, and if you like, do it again each night for eight nights as you clear that one space. Day seven hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights by lighting a menorah; Christians meet the feast in John 10:22, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians read 1 Maccabees as scripture, while some Protestants read it among the Apocrypha.

fork.setup: you're rebuilding the altar. the old one was defiled, but its stones were holy once. what do you do with them?
options: use them again in the new altar.
throw them out with the rubble.
store them until a prophet comes to say what to do.
fork.reveal: they laid the stones up on the temple mount until a prophet should come. they didn't pretend to know.

original.note: Hebrew: dedication, the name of the eight-day feast that remembers the altar rededicated.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanukkah is about a jar of oil.
what it means: a defiled temple is mourned, cleansed and given back to God, and the people keep eight days of dedication every year.
what a scholar hears: 1 Maccabees 4 gives the feast without the oil story, and John 10:22 calls it the feast of the dedication.

notes: All of 1 Maccabees is paraphrased; the writer was not certain of the exact KJV Apocrypha or Douay wording.
'Hanukkah means dedication' is the standard sense of חֲנֻכָּה and matches John's 'feast of the dedication'; confirm under the claims rule.
The oil story (Talmud, Shabbat 21b) is described only as 'a later Jewish tradition' that 1 Maccabees doesn't tell; confirm this framing is respectful to Jewish readers.
'Jews keep it to this day, lighting lights for eight nights' is a neighbor's practice, described briefly; confirm.
Canon: 1 Maccabees in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; 'some Protestant Bibles print it among the Apocrypha'. Confirm.
Antiochus's desecration summarized from 1 Maccabees 1:47, 1:54; Judas called Maccabeus from 2:4.
Carry suggests lighting one light for eight nights (the outline's practice); not a Hanukkah ritual imposed on Christians. Confirm tone.
Editor pass: 'as if every reader would know' cut; 'Jews keep it to this day' (not in the cited text) changed to 'Jewish tradition keeps it'.

Audit: hook said the resistance was 'led by Judas'; 1 Maccabees 2 has Mattathias and his sons begin it, with Judas leading after his father's death (3:1). Now 'a priest named Mattathias and his sons resisted, and in time his son Judas, called Maccabeus, led them'; source 1 Maccabees 2:1–5, 3:1 is covered by the paraphrase entry.
